concepts.title: Mass Media as a Social Institution
concepts.definition: Television, newspapers, films, magazines, radio, advertisements, video games and cds count as mass media because they reach enormous audiences at once. Unlike a chat between friends, mass communication needs a formally organised structure with big capital, production plants and management, which is why the state and the market dominate it. Media and society shape each other in both directions, and sections of the public differ sharply in how easily they can use media - the digital divide.
concepts.key_idea: Like any social institution, media changes its structure and content with the economic, political and socio-cultural setting - the state led in the early decades after independence, the market took over after the 1990s.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, introduction (four sociological aspects of media growth; dialectical relationship; digital divide)

concepts.title: Print Beginnings and the Imagined Community
concepts.section: 7.1 The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media
concepts.definition: Modern mass media started with johann gutenberg's printing press of 1440, first used for religious books; industrial growth, better transport and rising literacy carried newspapers to a mass public only by the mid-nineteenth century. Benedict anderson argued that reading or hearing the same news gave strangers a shared belonging - he called the nation an imagined community - and india's nationalist press, punished by censorship during the 1883 ilbert bill agitation, nurtured anti-colonial opinion.
concepts.key_idea: Papers like kesari, mathrubhumi and amrita bazar patrika suffered the colonial state's displeasure yet kept demanding an end to colonial rule, and their influence outran their small circulation through word of mouth in markets, courts and towns.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.1 (gutenberg 1440; benedict anderson; ilbert bill 1883; box 7.1 early newspapers)

concepts.title: Media as Watchdog in the Development Decades
concepts.section: 7.2 Mass Media in Independent India - The Approach
concepts.definition: Jawaharlal nehru wanted the free press to act as democracy's watchdog and a partner in national development: informing citizens about development efforts, attacking untouchability, child marriage, the ostracism of widows, witchcraft beliefs and faith healing, and promoting a rational scientific ethos. The state's films division made newsreels and documentaries shown before every feature film, and all india radio ran a decade-long countryside campaign on high-yielding varieties from 1967.
concepts.key_idea: Crises pushed air to grow - the 1962 china war brought a daily talks unit, the 1971 bangladesh crisis brought hourly news from 6 am to midnight, and the 1991 assassination of rajiv gandhi brought round-the-clock bulletins.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.2 the approach; box 7.2 green revolution campaign; box 7.3 wars and tragedies expanding air

concepts.title: Radio Reach Arithmetic at Independence
concepts.section: 7.2 Mass Media in Independent India - Radio
concepts.definition: Radio grew from amateur ham clubs in kolkata and chennai in the 1920s into a wartime propaganda instrument and then a public broadcasting system. At independence there were six radio stations, 280,000 receiver sets and 350 million people - fewer than one set per thousand - while by 1950 licences had reached 5,46,200, and by 2000 about 110 million households, two-thirds of all indian homes, listened in 24 languages and 146 dialects.
concepts.key_idea: The transistor revolution of the 1960s made sets mobile, battery-run and far cheaper, and air has since grown to 480 stations and 681 transmitters covering 99 percent of the people across 92 percent of the land.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.2 radio (1947: six stations, 280,000 sets, 350 million people; 1950: 5,46,200 licences; 2000: 110 million households)

concepts.title: Television from SITE to the Epics
concepts.section: 7.2 Mass Media in Independent India - Television
concepts.definition: Television began experimentally in 1959 to promote rural development; the satellite instructional television experiment (site) then beamed four hours of programmes daily to 2,400 community sets across six states between august 1975 and july 1976. Doordarshan stations stood in four cities by 1975 with three more added within a year, colour transmission arrived with the 1982 asian games, and the first long-running hindi soap hum log (1984-85, 156 episodes) drew about 50 million viewers a broadcast, ahead of buniyaad, ramayana and mahabharata.
concepts.key_idea: Once programmes could carry sponsor advertisements, entertainment aimed at the urban consuming class expanded and doordarshan earned heavy advertising revenue - the maggi noodles campaign rode in on hum log.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.2 television (1959 start; site 1975-76; 1982 asian games colour; box 7.4 hum log; box 7.5 maggi)

concepts.title: Satellite Television Homes and Viewers Growth
concepts.definition: Private satellite television exploded after star tv and zee tv arrived in 1991-92: weekly satellite viewers climbed from 134 million in 2002 to 190 million in 2005, homes with satellite access jumped from 40 million to 61 million over the same years, and satellite subscription now reaches 56 percent of all tv homes - with india, per trai, holding the world's second largest tv market after china.
concepts.key_idea: From a single state channel in 1991 to almost 70 channels by 1998, doordarshan's 35-plus channels now share the air with roughly 900 private networks broadcasting in 2020.

concepts.title: Cable Television Operator Growth Chain
concepts.definition: While doordarshan expanded in the 1980s, cable television mushroomed in the big cities: vcrs multiplied viewing choices, and by 1984 entrepreneurs in mumbai and ahmedabad were wiring apartment buildings to screen several films a day. The number of cable operators exploded from 100 in 1984 to 1,200 in 1988, 15,000 in 1992 and about 60,000 by 1999 - a six-hundredfold multiplication in fifteen years.
concepts.key_idea: Each interval of the chain roughly multiplied the operators a dozen-fold - twelve times by 1988, twelve and a half times by 1992, four times more by 1999.

concepts.title: Indian Language Newspaper Revolution and CAGR
concepts.section: 7.3 Globalisation and the Media - Print Media (Box 7.8)
concepts.definition: Contrary to predictions of print's decline, indian language newspapers boomed - hindi, telugu and kannada grew fastest. Average daily circulation rose from 39.1 million copies in 2006 to 62.8 million in 2016, an addition of 23.7 million copies, which the audit bureau reports as a compound annual growth rate of 4.87 percent; the north zone led at 7.83 percent while the south, west and east grew 4.95, 2.81 and 2.63 percent.
concepts.key_idea: Working the compound rate out from the two circulation totals reproduces the published figure - the ratio of about 1.61 over ten years compounds to roughly 4.9 percent a year.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.3 print media, box 7.8 (39.1 million 2006 to 62.8 million 2016, cagr 4.87 percent, zones 7.83/4.95/2.81/2.63)

concepts.title: Hindi Belt Migration and the Delhi Newspaper Market
concepts.section: 7.3 Globalisation and the Media - Print Media
concepts.definition: Migrants power the indian language press: of delhi's population of about one crore forty-seven lakh, 52 percent came from the hindi belt of uttar pradesh and bihar, and of these migrants 47 percent have rural roots while 60 percent are under forty. This is why the hindustan's delhi edition could leap from 64,000 copies in 2003 to 425,000 by 2005, and why papers like malayala manorama and eenadu built district and block editions for small-town readers.
concepts.key_idea: Indian language papers serve needs city papers ignore - local news, colloquial language, consumer contact programmes and door-to-door surveys - which is how dainik bhaskar and eenadu conquered the hinterland.

concepts.title: Transnational Channels and the Localisation Strategy
concepts.definition: Until the 1970s media firms worked within national markets and separate sectors; globalisation fused once-distinct forms and threw the industry open. The gulf war of 1991 popularised cnn, star tv launched that year and zee tv followed in 1992; transnational players learned that the familiar sells best - sony began with ten hindi films a week, mtv india added hindi programming, star sports took hindi commentary, and star plus converted entirely to hindi by february 1999 with the slogan aapki boli, aapka plus point.
concepts.key_idea: By 2000 forty private cable and satellite channels were available, several broadcasting only in regional languages such as sun tv, eenadu tv, udaya tv, raj tv and asianet, while zee built marathi and bengali networks.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.3 television (star tv 1991, zee tv 1992, sony's ten hindi films a week, star plus october 1996 to february 1999, box 7.7 music)

concepts.title: Infotainment, 24x7 News and the Voyeurism Debate
concepts.definition: Segmented reading habits pushed newspapers towards infotainment - a blend of information and entertainment - turning the paper into a consumer product where big numbers decide what sells. Television channels now run round the clock with lively informal news, fostering public debate yet raising the worry that serious political and economic issues get sidelined, as in the live rescue of little prince, where two channels suspended everything for two days and asked viewers to send sms messages.
concepts.key_idea: The prince rescue in kurukshetra - a 5-year-old trapped in a 55-ft borewell for 50 hours - split opinion between praising television for highlighting rural distress and condemning cameras for voyeurism into private moments.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.3 print and television (box 7.11 infotainment; 24x7 news; box 7.12 the rescue of prince)

concepts.title: FM Radio and Community Broadcasting
concepts.definition: Privately owned fm stations, allowed from 2002, turned radio towards entertainment: barred from political news bulletins, they specialise in popular music for young urban listeners, and big media houses own them - radio mirchi belongs to the times of india group, red fm to living media, radio city to the star network - while an independent public radio like npr or the bbc is missing from india. In bihar, raghav mahato's mansoorpur fm shows community radio's promise: a 50-rupee transmission kit, a 20 km radius and twelve hours of songs and local alerts daily.
concepts.key_idea: Raghav's shack station - films songs, hiv and polio messages, missing-children alerts and bhojpuri devotional songs at dawn and dusk - won more listeners than local politicians, though it runs without a government license.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy207.txt, section 7.3 radio (fm from 2002, ownership of mirchi/red fm/radio city, box 7.14 raghav fm mansoorpur 1)
